prompt: What is the octet 11000000 in decimal?
hint: Add the place values of the two ones.

prompt: Written as eight bits, the decimal number 200 is ___
Put the steps of converting 200 to binary in order.
hint: Start from the largest place value.
trap: Starting from the small values gets the bits in the wrong order: the method subtracts the largest value that fits first.

prompt: ipcalc printed pc1's address as 00001010.00010100.00001010. 00010101, with a space before the last octet. What does the space mark?
hint: Compare it with the Netmask line.

choices.text: The end of the private part of the address
choices.why: It is not about private ranges: ipcalc puts the space where the mask ends.

choices.text: Where the mask's 24 ones end
choices.why: Right. Left of it is the network part, right of it the host part.

choices.text: An octet ipcalc failed to convert
choices.why: The octet converted fine: 00010101 is 21.

choices.text: The byte the router rewrites on the way out
choices.why: NAT rewrites the whole source address, and ipcalc knows nothing about the router.

prompt: A packet from pc1 carries the source address 10.20.10.21. What is actually in the header?
hint: The dotted form is for people.

choices.text: Eleven characters of text, dots included
choices.why: Text would take eleven bytes; the header field is four bytes.

choices.text: Four numbers with a separator byte between them
choices.why: There is no separator: the four octets sit next to each other.

choices.text: The address together with its /24 mask
choices.why: The mask is not carried in the packet; each machine holds its own.

choices.text: 32 bits
choices.why: Right. Four octets, side by side, with no dots.

prompt: Under the old classful rules, which class is 172.16.5.4?
hint: Look at the first octet.

choices.text: Class A
choices.why: Class A ends at 127.

choices.text: Class C
choices.why: Class C starts at 192.

choices.text: Class B
choices.why: Right. 172 is between 128 and 191.

choices.text: Class D
choices.why: Class D is 224 to 239, the multicast groups.

prompt: Match the first bits of an address to its old class.
hint: Each extra leading 1 moves one class down the alphabet.

prompt: ipcalc -b 172.16.5.4 printed Class B beside the network 172.16.5.0/24. Why a /24 for a class B address?
hint: What happened with 10.1.2.3 and 192.168.1.1?

choices.text: This ipcalc assumes /24 when no mask is given
choices.why: Right. It printed /24 for the class A and C addresses too.

choices.text: A class B network is a /24
choices.why: A class B network had a 16-bit network part, a /16.

choices.text: 172.16.5.0/24 is one of the RFC 1918 blocks
choices.why: The private block is 172.16.0.0/12; ipcalc did not read the mask from it.

choices.text: pc1's own mask, /24, was applied to it
choices.why: ipcalc does not read pc1's interface; it calculates from what it is given.

prompt: In 1990, with classful addressing, an organisation needed addresses for 300 machines. What did it get?
hint: Count the hosts in each class.

choices.text: A class C with a longer mask
choices.why: Classful addressing had no mask to choose: a C was 254 hosts, too few.

choices.text: Two class C networks reached by one route
choices.why: Each class C was a route of its own, which is the second problem CIDR solved.

choices.text: A class B, leaving over 65,000 addresses unused
choices.why: Right. 65,534 hosts for 300 machines.

choices.text: A /23 of 510 hosts
choices.why: That is what CIDR allows after 1993.

prompt: ipcalc -b 224.0.0.5 printed Class D, Multicast, and also HostMin 224.0.0.1 and HostMax 224.0.0.254. What should you make of those two lines?
hint: What is inside a multicast address?

choices.text: They are the group's first and last members
choices.why: Members join a group by its address; they have their own unicast addresses.

choices.text: They are the range OSPF routers use
choices.why: OSPF uses the group 224.0.0.5 itself, not a range of hosts.

choices.text: Ignore them, since a group has no hosts inside
choices.why: Right. ipcalc applied /24 arithmetic because it was asked to.

choices.text: They show multicast is limited to 254 receivers
choices.why: A group has no such limit; the numbers are /24 arithmetic.

prompt: Which of these addresses are private, in the RFC 1918 sense? Choose all that apply.

choices.why: 172.16/12 runs to 172.31, so 172.20 is inside.
One past the end of 172.16/12: an ordinary public address.
Shared address space for carrier-grade NAT, RFC 6598, a different block.

prompt: A web server outside the office logs a visit from pc1. Which source address does its log show?
hint: Which address does a packet leave the office with?

choices.why: pc1's private address is rewritten on the way out.
That is r1's inside address, the office's gateway.
Right. r1's outside address is the source of everything the office sends out.
That is the provider's end of the link.

prompt: A home router shows 100.72.14.9 on its outside interface. What does that tell you?
hint: Which block is 100.72 in?

choices.text: It is a public class A address, reachable from the internet
choices.why: ipcalc would say Class A, but the block is 100.64.0.0/10, shared space.

choices.text: The provider runs a second NAT in front of the home
choices.why: Right. Shared address space sits between customers and the provider's NAT.

choices.text: It is a documentation address, so the router is in a lab
choices.why: Documentation blocks are 192.0.2, 198.51.100 and 203.0.113.

choices.text: It is link-local: the router failed to reach DHCP
choices.why: Link-local addresses start with 169.254.

prompt: RFC 5737 sets aside 192.0.2.0/24, 198.51.100.0/24 and 203.0.113.0/24 so books and labs can print addresses that belong to nobody. They are the ___ blocks.
hint: What this lab uses them for.

prompt: The private block 172.16.0.0/12 starts at 172.16.0.0. What is the second octet of its last address?
hint: A /12 leaves four bits of the second octet free.

prompt: Nothing on pc1 was given 127.45.6.7, yet ping 127.45.6.7 answered. Why?
hint: Read the mask on lo.

choices.text: r1 answers for unknown addresses
choices.why: The reply never left pc1; r1 was not involved.
Right. The /8 covers 127.45.6.7, so the kernel answers for it.

choices.text: ping rewrote the address to 127.0.0.1
choices.why: The output shows replies from 127.45.6.7 itself.

choices.text: Linux treats 127.x.x.x as a broadcast
choices.why: It is loopback, not broadcast: one machine, no network.

prompt: A user's network cable is unplugged. They run ping 127.0.0.1. What happens?
hint: Where does a loopback packet go?

choices.text: It answers, as it would with the cable in
choices.why: Right. Loopback never touches the card, so it tells you nothing about the cable.

choices.text: Network is unreachable
choices.why: That message is about routes to other networks; lo has its own.

choices.text: 100% packet loss, because the card is down
choices.why: The card is not on the path of a loopback packet.

choices.text: A reply from the switch port
choices.why: The packet does not leave the machine.

prompt: A database answers when tested on its own server, but the web server on another machine gets Connection refused. ss on the database server shows LISTEN on 127.0.0.1:5432. What is wrong?
hint: Who can reach an address with scope host?

choices.text: Port 5432 is blocked by the switch
choices.why: A switch forwards frames by MAC address and does not look at ports.

choices.text: The web server is on the wrong subnet
choices.why: A wrong subnet gives no route or no answer, not an immediate refusal from the server.

choices.text: It listens on loopback, which nothing outside reaches
choices.why: Right. It needs to listen on the server's real address, or on 0.0.0.0.

choices.text: 127.0.0.1 is a private address and is filtered by NAT
choices.why: Loopback is not RFC 1918 space, and no NAT sits between two machines on one LAN.

prompt: pc1's first ping -b to 10.20.10.255 reported 100% packet loss. What happened to the two requests?
hint: Read pc2's sysctl.

choices.text: r1 dropped them before they reached the switch
choices.why: pc1 and the others share sw1; r1 is not on the path.

choices.text: Everybody received them and chose not to answer
choices.why: Right. icmp_echo_ignore_broadcasts = 1 is the default.

choices.text: 10.20.10.255 is not a valid address in a /24
choices.why: It is the network's directed broadcast, and ping sent to it.

choices.text: ping needs root to send a broadcast
choices.why: ana sent it with -b; the replies were missing, not the requests.

prompt: After pc2 and pc3 changed the setting, ping -b sent 2 requests and reported 2 received, +1 duplicates. How many echo replies arrived in all?
hint: Duplicates are extra replies to the same request.

prompt: The directed broadcast address of 10.20.10.0/24 is 10.20.10.___
hint: Every host bit set to 1.

prompt: Why do routers drop a directed broadcast that arrives from another network, instead of delivering it?
hint: Think about who would answer, and to whom.

choices.text: Because the sender's MAC address is unknown on the far network
choices.why: The router would put its own MAC on the frame; that is ordinary forwarding.

choices.text: Because a broadcast address is not routable at all
choices.why: 10.20.10.255 is an ordinary destination as far as a routing table is concerned.

choices.text: So one forged packet cannot make a whole network answer a victim
choices.why: Right. That was the smurf attack, and RFC 2644 made dropping the default.

choices.text: To save the bandwidth of the link
choices.why: Bandwidth is a side effect; the reason is the amplification.

prompt: A PC in the office shows the address 169.254.33.7. What is the first thing it tells you?
hint: Who picked that address?

choices.text: The PC is on the internet with a class B address
choices.why: ipcalc says Class B, but the class means nothing for this range.

choices.text: The PC is behind the provider's NAT
choices.why: That would be 100.64.0.0/10, on the router's outside.

choices.text: Somebody typed a documentation address
choices.why: Documentation blocks are 192.0.2, 198.51.100 and 203.0.113.

choices.text: It asked DHCP and got no answer
choices.why: Right. 169.254 is the address a machine picks for itself; lesson 10 finds out why.

prompt: Match each range to what it is.
hint: The table at the end of the section.

prompt: On srv, ss -tln shows LISTEN on 10.20.10.10:80 with the peer column 0.0.0.0:*. What does 0.0.0.0:* say?
hint: The peer is the other end of a connection.

choices.text: srv has no address yet
choices.why: srv's own address is in the Local column: 10.20.10.10.

choices.text: Any address on any port is welcome to connect
choices.why: Right. In a socket list 0.0.0.0 means any.

choices.text: The server is listening on every address it has
choices.why: That would be 0.0.0.0:80 in the Local column.

choices.text: Connections arrive from the default route
choices.why: Routes do not appear in ss; this is the socket's view.

prompt: ip route get 8.8.8.8 answered 8.8.8.8 via 10.20.10.1 dev eth0. A packet for that address would be handed to the ___
Under the old rules, class C starts with the bits 110. What is the highest first octet a class C address can have?
hint: 110 followed by five ones.

prompt: Which of these addresses could be configured on a new PC in 10.20.10.0/24?
hint: Two addresses of every network are not for machines.

choices.why: The network address: every host bit is 0.
The broadcast address: every host bit is 1.
Another network: the third octet differs.
Right. HostMax, the last usable address.

prompt: How many addresses does the loopback block 127.0.0.0/8 hold?
hint: Two to the power of the host bits.

prompt: A machine with its cable unplugged still answers a ping to 127.0.0.1, because that address belongs to the ___ interface.
hint: Its name is lo.
